analysis.one_liner: Lets House candidates opt into public campaign financing funded by small donors instead of large contributions.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2011 with 102 cosponsors, the bill sat in the House Administration Committee without a hearing or vote until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Elections Now Act would have created a voluntary system for financing House campaigns with public money. Candidates who gathered enough small contributions from their own state ($5-$100 checks) would get a government grant plus a 500% match on small-dollar donations, and in exchange they could no longer take large contributions or spend their own money. The goal was to let candidates win office without relying on wealthy donors and lobbyists, and to reduce the appearance that legislation is shaped by the people who fund campaigns. It also required participating candidates to hold public debates and required all campaign filings to be electronic and posted online within 24 hours.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates without access to wealthy donor networks — challengers, candidates of modest means, and anyone not already connected to the moneyed establishment — could run competitive campaigns funded by small contributions from ordinary voters. Small donors would see their gifts multiplied five-fold. Voters would get guaranteed public debates and faster, searchable disclosure of campaign filings, and the bill's own findings argue the change could reduce legislative outcomes skewed toward large contributors.

how_it_helps.text: A certified participating candidate receives a primary allocation of 40% and a general election allocation of 60% of a base amount set at 80% of the average spending of recent winning House candidates, plus a 500% match on small contributions from in-state residents.

To qualify, a candidate must collect contributions from at least 1,500 individuals (or 0.25% of the state's voting-age population, whichever is smaller) totaling at least $50,000, in amounts between $5 and $100, proving a real base of local support before any public money flows.

Once certified, the candidate may accept no contributions other than the small qualifying contributions, the matched small-dollar gifts, and the fund payments, and may not spend personal or immediate-family money — replacing large private donations with small-donor and public money.

Participating candidates must take part in at least one public debate before the primary and two before the general election, and unspent public funds must be returned to the Fair Elections Fund within 60 days after the election.

The bill requires all campaign reports to be filed electronically with the FEC and posted publicly within 24 hours of receipt, instead of the previous 48-hour deadline, and bars registered lobbyists from serving on the program's oversight board.

The bill's stated findings are that private campaign financing fosters conflicts of interest, makes legislators accountable to major contributors rather than constituents, and imposes costs on taxpayers through legislative outcomes skewed by contributor access.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the program: the Fair Elections Fund is financed by appropriations (the bill authorizes 'such sums as are necessary'), voluntary checkoff contributions, and 50% of FEC civil penalties. Incumbent members and party committees would lose their current fundraising advantages — participating candidates are barred from large contributions and joint fundraising committees, and coordinated party spending on their behalf is capped at 10% of the general-election allocation. Large donors and lobbyists would lose their most direct channel of influence over House members.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, large donors, and incumbent fundraisers

drawbacks.text: The program is open-ended for taxpayers: the bill authorizes appropriations of 'such sums as are necessary' to the Fair Elections Fund, with no fixed spending cap, and the base payment amounts rise automatically with the average spending of winning candidates.

Participation is voluntary, and after the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision outside groups could still spend unlimited independent money against a candidate who accepts the program's spending structure, so opponents argued it could disarm one side while leaving the battlefield unchanged.

The base amount is tied to 80% of recent winners' average spending, which disadvantages candidates in expensive media markets and locks in ever-rising campaign costs rather than pushing spending down.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is structural: candidates could win House seats on $5-$100 contributions from their own constituents, weakening the tie between members and their largest donors. The costs are real but bounded and debated — a multi-hundred-million-dollar annual federal outlay, a spending framework that may not keep pace with outside independent spending, and a formula pegged to past campaign spending rather than actual need. A fair reading is that the trade-off — public money in exchange for publicly accountable campaigns — was the explicit deal the bill offered, and the objections were mostly about design details and cost, not the premise.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died at the end of the 112th Congress without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: H.R. 1404 was introduced on April 6, 2011 by Rep. John Larson with 45 original cosponsors and referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration.
It ultimately drew 102 cosponsors — 101 Democrats and 1 Republican — but the action history ends with the referral; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and all bills not passed by then expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and their large donors came out ahead: the existing private-financing system, which the bill's own findings described as fostering contributor access and skewing legislative agendas, continued unchanged, while a bill backed by 102 members died without ever being debated.

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson

for.name: Rep. Chellie Pingree
for.role: U.S. Representative (ME-1); original cosponsor and leading advocate of public campaign financing

for.name: 101 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority-of-caucus support but no path to the floor under Republican control.

against.name: Rep. Daniel Lungren

against.name: Speaker John Boehner
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote during the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic — 101 of 102 cosponsors were Democrats, with a single Republican — and the bill received no Republican-controlled committee action or floor vote.

industries.industry: Large-dollar campaign donors, lobbying firms, and industry PACs
industries.note: The bill would have cut them off as the financing channel for House campaigns: certified candidates could accept only small in-state contributions, and the oversight board was barred from seating registered lobbyists. Their loss was precisely the access and influence over lawmakers that public financing aimed to eliminate.

Participating candidates could no longer form joint fundraising committees with party committees, and coordinated party spending on their behalf was capped at 10% of the general-election allocation. Parties would still be free to spend independently on behalf of non-participating candidates.

Television and digital advertising are the largest expense in House campaigns; a publicly financed system pegged to past spending levels would not expand — and could constrain — the advertising budgets broadcasters and media firms depend on each election cycle.

industries.industry: Political fundraising and campaign consulting firms
industries.note: The bill banned paying commissions to people who collect qualifying contributions, barred participating candidates' funds from uses beyond their own campaigns, and tightened disclosure, shrinking the market for high-dollar fundraising operations.
